source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: a holistic framework to evaluate AI agents for autonomous clouds
finding: Benchmark that mirrors the troubleshooting cycle in four levels: detect, localize, root-cause analyse, mitigate. Four LLM agents were run on 48 injected-fault problems in microservice clouds.
numbers: Overall accuracy: FLASH 59.32%, ReAct 55.93%, GPT-4 with shell 49.15%, GPT-3.5 with shell 15.25% (step limit 20 for the best run).
limits: Simulated faults on a few open-source apps; table text was garbled in extraction so per-agent overall values are read from the table order.
agent_relevance: The four levels match S1 to S4 plus repair. The schema can be scored per level, not only on the final fix.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: a holistic framework to evaluate AI agents for autonomous clouds
finding: Hard levels are root cause and mitigation. Easy-looking detection (yes/no) was not solved by most agents.
numbers: Detection: GPT-4-shell 69.23%, GPT-3.5-shell 23.07%, ReAct 76.92%, FLASH 100%. RCA: GPT-4-shell 40.90%, GPT-3.5-shell 9.09%, ReAct 45.45%, FLASH 36.36%. Mitigation: GPT-4-shell 27.27%, GPT-3.5-shell 0%.
limits: Small N per level (about 11 to 13 problems).
agent_relevance: Accuracy falls from detect to cause to fix. The cause step (S3/S4) is the weak link, so it needs a check, not trust.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: a holistic framework to evaluate AI agents for autonomous clouds
finding: Localization: all LLM agents beat classic non-LLM AIOps methods, but top-1 versus top-3 differs a lot.
numbers: Localization acc@1 / acc@3: GPT-4-shell 61.54/61.54, ReAct 53.85/69.23, FLASH 46.15/61.54; PDiagnose 15.38/15.38, RMLAD 7.69/7.69.
limits: Classic baselines were adapted to the setting.
agent_relevance: Ranked hypotheses help: keep a short list of candidate causes and test them, rather than commit to one.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: a holistic framework to evaluate AI agents for autonomous clouds
finding: More steps help only for some agents. Agents waste steps repeating the same API call, invent non-existent APIs, and flood context with raw telemetry.
numbers: FLASH reached its best 59.32% at a step limit of 20; GPT-3.5 stopped improving after a certain number of steps.
agent_relevance: Two guardrail hints: cap and de-duplicate repeated actions, and filter data before it enters context.

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab: a holistic framework to evaluate AI agents for autonomous clouds
finding: Agents misread normal activity (e.g. standard workload generation) as a fault.
numbers: On no-fault (Noop) problems only GPT-4-shell answered correctly; the other agents reported false positives.
limits: Number of Noop problems is small.
agent_relevance: Supports G3: a pass needs a test that could have failed, including a healthy-system control.

source: Roy et al. (2024) Exploring LLM-based agents for root cause analysis
finding: ReAct agent with retrieval tools was compared with retrieval-based (RB, k=10) and chain-of-thought baselines on real production incidents.
numbers: Correctness: baselines (CoT and RB k=10) 39%; ReAct with retrieval 35%. Hallucinated content in correct predictions: 26% (10/38) for RB k=10, under 1% for CoT and ReAct. In wrong predictions: 18% (11/59) CoT and 6% (4/63) ReAct.
limits: Single company, out-of-distribution incidents, text-similarity metrics; hallucination counts hand-coded; attribution of the 18%/6% figures is read from garbled text.
agent_relevance: Tool-using agents trade a little correctness for much more factual grounding. Grounding in observed output is the point of G2.

source: Roy et al. (2024) Exploring LLM-based agents for root cause analysis
finding: Adding human discussion threads from the incident as extra input did not give significant gains.
numbers: No significant improvement for the tested models; ReAct variants mostly gained slightly, CoT did not.
quote: surprisingly does not yield significant performance improvements
limits: Authors' own words; metrics BLEU, METEOR, ROUGE.
agent_relevance: More text is not more evidence. Fresh, targeted observations beat piled-up context.

source: Roy et al. (2024) Exploring LLM-based agents for root cause analysis
finding: A case study with a Microsoft team gave the agent the team's own diagnostic services as tools, so it could gather data on demand.
numbers: Qualitative case study; no headline number read.
agent_relevance: Open data sources inside the loop is the S1 to S4 support in the task brief.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Automatic root cause analysis via LLMs for cloud incidents (RCACopilot)
finding: Handler workflow collects diagnostic data per incident type, then an LLM predicts the root-cause category using similar past incidents.
numbers: Micro-F1 0.766 and Macro-F1 0.533 (GPT-4); GPT-3.5 version Micro-F1 0.761, Macro-F1 0.505. About a year of Microsoft incidents, 25% test split.
limits: Category labels from one company; a GPT-4 embedding baseline scored far lower.
agent_relevance: A fixed collection step before the LLM reasons (observe first, then hypothesise) beats raw prompting.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Automatic root cause analysis via LLMs for cloud incidents (RCACopilot)
finding: Results were repeated over three rounds and the system is described as in use by on-call engineers for years.
numbers: Three rounds, Micro-F1 consistently high.
agent_relevance: Repeat runs check stability but not independence (G4).

source: Wang et al. (2024) RCAgent: cloud root cause analysis by autonomous agents with tool-augmented LLMs
finding: Tool agent with self-consistency over action trajectories, context management and domain knowledge beats ReAct on root cause, solution, evidence and responsible-party prediction.
numbers: Gain on solution prediction of +3.51 METEOR and +4.50 BLEURT over ReAct; the full table was not read.
limits: Internal Alibaba model and data; automated plus human checks.
agent_relevance: Voting over trajectories helps here, but G4 warns the votes are correlated.

source: Jha et al. (2025) ITBench: evaluating AI agents across diverse real-world IT automation tasks
finding: 94 real-world scenarios across SRE (42), CISO (50) and FinOps (2). Agents solved few.
numbers: Handling rates: SRE 13.8%, CISO 25.2%.
agent_relevance: Real faults are far harder than curated ones. Expect a big drop outside clean benchmarks.

source: Jha et al. (2025) ITBench: evaluating AI agents across diverse real-world IT automation tasks
finding: On SRE scenarios, GPT-4o was best, but diagnosis was still low and data type changed results.
numbers: GPT-4o diagnosis pass@1 13.81% and mitigation about 11% (value partly cut in extraction); in the FinOps study its diagnosis pass@1 fell when the data type changed.
agent_relevance: Diagnosing the origin is still the bottleneck, even with open tools.

source: Jha et al. (2025) ITBench: evaluating AI agents across diverse real-world IT automation tasks
finding: Metrics include fault-localisation (FL) and fault-propagation-chain (FPC) scores, plus time to detect and mitigate, not only final answer.
numbers: FL, FPC, MTTR, MTTD reported per model.
limits: Metric definitions taken from the paper.
agent_relevance: Score the chain of reasoning steps, not only the answer.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A quantitative and qualitative evaluation of LLM-based explainable fault localization (AutoFL)
finding: LLM navigates a code repo with function calls and writes a bug explanation plus a location. Tested on 798 real bugs (Java Defects4J, Python BugsInPy).
numbers: Method-level acc@1 up to 233.3% higher than baselines; with GPT-3.5 it beat spectrum-based and mutation-based techniques on Defects4J.
limits: Percentages are relative gains; training-data leakage is a risk.
agent_relevance: Program debugging is troubleshooting; open navigation tools plus an explanation is a usable S1 to S3 loop.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A quantitative and qualitative evaluation of LLM-based explainable fault localization (AutoFL)
finding: Developers were interviewed about the explanations.
numbers: Interview study; qualitative.
agent_relevance: Explanations are checkable by humans; useful as an audit trail.

source: Pei et al. (2025) Flow-of-Action: SOP enhanced LLM multi-agent system for root cause analysis
finding: Encoding the diagnosis steps of expert site reliability engineers as a standard operating procedure (SOP) raised accuracy sharply over free ReAct.
numbers: Accuracy with GPT-4-Turbo: Flow-of-Action 64.01%, ReAct 35.50%, CoT 32.61%, Reflexion 29.06%.
limits: Own dataset; the ablation that removed the SOP tooling made it revert to ReAct with sharply lower accuracy.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence that a structured expert procedure (like Schaafstal's structured troubleshooting) helps inside an LLM loop.

source: Pei et al. (2025) Flow-of-Action: SOP enhanced LLM multi-agent system for root cause analysis
finding: Helper agents prune noise, narrow the search space and decide when to stop; removing the action set hurt most.
numbers: Ablation: action set removal cut accuracy most; other ablations were similar in size.
agent_relevance: Code-decided stop and narrowing support G1: act on signals, not schedules.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Without external feedback, asking a model to check its answer makes it worse or no better.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0 to 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CSQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0 (rounds 0, 1, 2).
agent_relevance: Supports G2: revise only from real output, not from the model's own review of its cause.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: With oracle labels the same loop looked strong, so the gain came from the label, not the reasoning.
numbers: GPT-4 with oracle: GSM8K 97.5, CSQA 85.5, HotpotQA 59.0 versus 95.5, 82.0, 49.0 without.
agent_relevance: A real test result plays the role of the oracle in troubleshooting.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Models change correct answers to wrong ones more often than the reverse on some sets.
numbers: Authors report correct-to-incorrect switches outweigh incorrect-to-correct on GSM8K.
agent_relevance: Do not let the model overturn a validated finding on opinion.

source: Savage et al. (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for LLM interpretability in medicine
finding: Prompts that imitate clinician reasoning (differential diagnosis, intuitive, analytic, Bayesian) on a 497-question MedQA subset.
numbers: GPT-4 accuracy: CoT 76%, intuitive 77%, differential 78%, analytic 78%, Bayesian 72% (none significant; Bayesian P=0.07).
agent_relevance: A strong model can follow a diagnostic procedure without losing accuracy and gives a readable rationale.

source: Savage et al. (2024) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for LLM interpretability in medicine
finding: The weaker model could not use the advanced reasoning styles.
numbers: GPT-3.5: CoT 46%, intuitive 48%; differential diagnosis 38% (diff -8%, P<0.001); Bayesian 42%.
agent_relevance: Procedure prompts help only if the model is strong enough; test per model.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: demystifying LLM-based software engineering agents
finding: A fixed three-phase pipeline (localize, repair, validate) with no model-chosen next step beat open agents on SWE-bench Lite.
numbers: 32.00% (96 of 300 issues) at $0.70 per issue, best among open-source agents at the time.
limits: SWE-bench Lite has leaked or vague items; authors built a cleaned Lite-S.
agent_relevance: Program-decided phases (guardrail section 1) matched or beat free agent choice, and cost less.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: demystifying LLM-based software engineering agents
finding: It generates reproduction tests that trigger the original error, then uses them with regression tests to pick among candidate patches.
numbers: Reproduction plus regression tests drive patch selection.
agent_relevance: Matches test-then-validate (S4): build a failing test first, then check the fix against it.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: Self-repair gains are modest once repair cost is counted; the bottleneck is the model's feedback on its own code.
numbers: Gains modest and sometimes absent on HumanEval and APPS; stronger-model feedback and expert-human feedback raised repair success clearly (exact human figure cut in extraction).
limits: Human feedback study is small (about 80 cases).
agent_relevance: Diagnosis quality is the limiter. Give the model real failing output, not its own critique.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: Human feedback shows uncertainty and high-level change ideas; GPT-4 never expressed uncertainty.
numbers: Uncertainty: humans 7/80, GPT-4 0/80. High-level change suggestions: 23/80 humans vs 18/80 GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Models do not flag doubt; uncertainty must come from code (disagreement, failed checks).

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (MAST)
finding: Failure taxonomy from 1600+ traces: 14 modes in three groups (system design, inter-agent misalignment, task verification). Several look like bad human troubleshooting.
numbers: Step repetition 15.7%, not recognizing task completion 12.4%, not following task requirements 11.8%, task derailment 7.4%, proceeding on wrong assumptions 6.8%. Annotator kappa 0.88.
limits: Based on multi-agent frameworks, not troubleshooting alone.
agent_relevance: Same failure shapes as weak troubleshooters: loops, no stop rule, no verification. Code-side stop and verify rules address them.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (MAST)
finding: Adding a high-level objective verification step improved task success.
numbers: +15.6% task success on ProgramDev with ChatDev.
agent_relevance: A final verification step is cheap and works.

source: Pham et al. (2025) RCAEval: a benchmark for root cause analysis of microservice systems
finding: Benchmark of 735 failure cases from three microservice systems with metrics, logs and traces, built to compare classic (non-LLM) RCA methods.
numbers: 735 cases in three datasets.
limits: LLM agents are not the focus; useful as a baseline and a held-out check set.
agent_relevance: A held-out set of real fault cases for testing any hypothesis-test loop.

source: Reiter (1987) A theory of diagnosis from first principles; de Kleer and Williams (1987) Diagnosing multiple faults
finding: Classic model-based diagnosis: compare observed behaviour with a model, derive minimal conflict sets, pick the next probe to cut candidate faults (GDE).
numbers: Not opened; no numbers quoted.
agent_relevance: The older formal version of S2 to S4: candidates from conflicts, then the most informative test.

source: Davis (1984) Diagnostic reasoning based on structure and behavior; Shortliffe MYCIN (1976)
finding: Expert systems for diagnosis: MYCIN used rules with certainty factors; Davis argued for reasoning from device structure rather than only symptoms.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers quoted.
agent_relevance: Rule-based experience versus first-principles reasoning mirrors novice versus expert troubleshooting.
